name: gcc
one_line: GNU project C and C++ compiler
plain: `gcc` turns C source code (text you can read) into a program the computer can run. You write hello.c, run gcc, and get an executable file.

In security work you use it to build practice programs, to see how C turns into assembly, to build programs with protections switched on or off for exploit practice, and to compile helper tools that a challenge ships as source code. gcc has thousands of options; this guide explains the ones you will actually use and when to reach for each.
when: Compile a C file from a challenge or tutorial so you can run it.
Build a vulnerable practice program with chosen protections (stack canary, executable stack, randomised addresses).
Look at the assembly the compiler produces for a line of C, to learn reverse engineering.
Build a program with debug information so gdb shows your source lines.
Find memory bugs in your own code with the sanitizers.

examples.title: Compile and run a program
examples.explain: gcc reads hello.c, compiles and links it, and -o hello names the result. The && runs ./hello only if the build worked. If you leave out -o, gcc names the file a.out. The leading ./ is needed because the current folder is not on your PATH.

examples.title: Turn on warnings
examples.explain: -Wall switches on the common warnings and -Wextra adds more. Warnings often point at real bugs: using an uninitialised variable, a printf format that does not match its argument, comparing a signed with an unsigned number. Add -Werror to make any warning stop the build.

examples.title: Build for the debugger
examples.explain: -g stores source line information in the program, so gdb can show your C code and let you break on a line. -O0 means no optimisation, so the machine code follows your source closely and variables do not disappear. Use this pair for learning and debugging.

examples.title: See the assembly the compiler writes
examples.explain: -S stops after compiling and writes assembly text to hello.s instead of building a program. -masm=intel prints it in Intel syntax (destination first), the style most books and tools use. Open hello.s in an editor and match each C line to its instructions. Add -O2 to see how optimisation changes the code.

examples.title: The four stages, one at a time
examples.cmd: gcc -E hello.c > hello.i;  gcc -S hello.c;  gcc -c hello.c;  gcc hello.o -o hello
examples.explain: -E only runs the preprocessor (it pastes #include files and expands #define, giving hello.i). -S compiles to assembly (hello.s). -c assembles to an object file (hello.o) without linking. The last command links the object file into a finished program. Knowing the stages helps you read error messages: a 'undefined reference' error comes from the link stage, a syntax error from the compile stage.

examples.title: Several source files
examples.explain: gcc compiles each .c file and links them together. For bigger projects compile each file with -c once and relink, which is what make does for you.

examples.title: Pass a macro on the command line
examples.explain: -DNAME=value acts like a #define at the top of every file. Programs often wrap debug prints in #ifdef DEBUG, so this switches them on without editing the source. Note the quote trick: the shell removes the outer single quotes, so the program sees the string "1.2".

examples.title: Use a library
examples.explain: -lNAME links the library libNAME (here OpenSSL's libcrypto and the maths library libm). Put -l options after the source files, or the linker may not use them. If the library's headers or files are in a non-standard place, add -I/path/include and -L/path/lib.

examples.title: Build a 32-bit program
examples.explain: -m32 builds a 32-bit program, the kind used by Narnia and many exploit tutorials; -m64 builds 64-bit. On Kali or Ubuntu you first need the 32-bit support files: sudo apt install gcc-multilib.

examples.title: A practice program with the protections off (exploit lab)
examples.explain: Modern gcc adds defences by default. This line removes them so a lab program behaves like the classic buffer-overflow examples. -fno-stack-protector removes the stack canary (a guard value before the return address). -z execstack marks the stack executable so shellcode placed there can run. -no-pie builds at a fixed address instead of a random one. Randomised stack addresses are also controlled by the kernel: on a lab machine only, sudo sysctl -w kernel.randomize_va_space=0 turns that off. Only do this to programs you own and on machines you control.

examples.title: A static program
examples.explain: -static copies the libraries into the program, so it does not depend on the system's libc. The file is much bigger, but it runs on machines with different libraries and has many more code snippets (gadgets) for ROP practice. file hello_static says 'statically linked'.

examples.title: Catch memory bugs while you test
examples.explain: The sanitizers add checks at run time. AddressSanitizer stops with a clear report when the program overruns a buffer, uses freed memory or reads outside an array; UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer catches things like integer overflow. It is the friendliest way to see a bug you are about to exploit.

examples.title: Keep the intermediate files
examples.explain: -save-temps keeps hello.i, hello.s and hello.o next to the program, so you get every stage in one command.

examples.title: Check what protections a program has
examples.cmd: readelf -lW vuln | grep GNU_STACK;  readelf -h vuln | grep Type
examples.explain: After compiling, confirm that you really got what you asked for. GNU_STACK with flags RWE means an executable stack; RW means it is not executable. Type EXEC means a fixed address (no PIE); DYN means position independent. The tool checksec shows all protections at once.

mistakes: Putting -l options before the source file: the linker may drop the library. Write gcc file.c -lm, not gcc -lm file.c.
Forgetting -m32 support: 'cannot find -lgcc' or missing bits/ headers means install gcc-multilib.
Expecting your lab program to be vulnerable after a normal build: modern gcc turns on protections, so you must switch them off explicitly.
Optimising a program and then being confused by the assembly: use -O0 while learning.
Ignoring warnings: in C they are often the bug.

captured_with: This is a focused guide: it explains the options used most in security study and everyday C work, not all of gcc's roughly 2,600 options. Examples are written to show a technique and are not captured output.
